items.caption:
Most videos lose people in the first 2 seconds because the hook sounds optional.

"Wanna know how?" lets people scroll.
"Your first 2 seconds are killing your views" makes them stop.

Tease, don't ask. A statement creates tension a question never will.

items.caption:
Auto-captions feel free. They're not.

They land a half-second late, miss the emphasis, and flatten the joke. People feel it before they can explain it, and they swipe.

Hand-place your words on the beat. Slower to do, sharper to watch.

items.caption:
If your hook runs longer than 1.5 seconds, the scroll already won.

The first beat is for the problem, stated sharp. No "hey guys." No setup. No throat-clearing.

Teaching starts at second 4. Second 1 is only for stopping the thumb.

items.caption:
Talking-head videos feel boring for one reason: you stood in one spot.

Same frame for 30 seconds and the brain checks out.

Switch location every line. New background each sentence. It reads as energy and pace even when the words are identical.

Follow @josephborroto for retention tricks that actually work.

That's the "why am I still watching this" moment. If nothing specific lands right there, they're gone.

The fix: a number, a name, or a contradiction at second 4. Specificity buys you the next 10 seconds.

items.caption:
Every short-form video that pops has 3 acts:

1. Hook (0 to 1.5s) — state the problem sharp
2. Tension (4 to 12s) — give a reason to stay
3. Payoff (13s to end) — deliver, then one clear close

Most people film all hook or all payoff. The tension in the middle is what holds people.

Follow @josephborroto for the structure behind the views.

items.caption:
Your B-roll is boring because you film the action instead of the thing.

Verbs: someone doing the task, wide and busy.
Nouns: the object itself, close-up, isolated, lit.

B-roll wins on detail, not motion. Get tight on the noun.

Follow @josephborroto for the small stuff that makes content look pro.

items.alt: Card: your B-roll is boring, you're filming verbs not nouns.

items.caption:
If you can clearly hear the music, it's too loud.

The voice leads. The music supports. Pull the track way lower than feels right, then a touch lower.

Clean audio is the difference between amateur and watchable, and most people get it backwards.

items.caption:
Most people frame too tight, then the on-screen title lands right on their face.

The fix takes one second: leave headroom. Frame with empty space above you so the title has somewhere to live.

Shoot for the overlay before you ever add it.

"How to edit faster" = scroll.
"I wasted 2 years editing the slow way" = stop.

Tease the gap in the first 2 seconds. Save the how-to for later in the video.

A comment means someone stopped, thought, and typed. That dwell time tells the algorithm the video held attention, and it pushes it to more people.

Reply to every comment in the first hour. It compounds.

Keep it clean and keep it in the safe zone so the app's UI never covers it.
